lead: Veterinary blood banks and oxygen therapeutics share a practical goal: support the patient when timely oxygen delivery is at risk.

paragraphs.text: In 2009, Veterinary Practice News described how blood-bank professionals viewed Oxyglobin as an oxygen bridge: a way to support patients while donor blood was being arranged. Cooperation with the donor-blood system was already central to its practical role.

That need remains relevant today. U.S. dog and cat ownership expanded in 2025, and a large veterinary-record study documented increasing life expectancy in dogs and cats between 2013 and 2018. Pet Blood Bank UK currently reports growing demand for blood and the need for more donors. We see these trends as further reasons to strengthen cooperation between blood banks, veterinary hospitals and oxygen-therapeutics developers.

As oxygen-delivery science advances, the therapeutic focus extends beyond the historical "blood substitute" label. Precision Oxygen Therapeutics centres on oxygen reaching tissues and cells, where it supports oxygen-dependent metabolism. This broader perspective connects transfusion care and veterinary emergency medicine with microvascular oxygen delivery and tissue function.

The oxygen bridge was the historical starting point. Today, our BHOC, Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier, development programme has a broader aim: sustained, controlled and physiologically responsive oxygen delivery during treatment, whether donor blood is available, delayed or already being transfused.

We aim to match oxygen unloading to local tissue conditions and metabolic demand: greater release where oxygen tension is low, and less where oxygen is sufficient. This extends the research focus to the interaction between oxygen transport, microvascular blood flow and cellular metabolism.

Our research priorities include supporting oxygen-dependent immune function; investigating whether iron recovered from carrier hemoglobin can contribute to endogenous erythropoiesis; and testing improvements in wound healing and the quality and speed of rehabilitation. These are product- and species-specific research aims.

We welcome collaboration with veterinary blood banks and clinical teams to define research priorities and evaluate how this approach could strengthen care. The shared objective is timely oxygen support for the patient, with donor blood and oxygen therapeutics contributing through their respective functions.

references.detail: Physiological review, 2003. Oxygen transport and microcirculatory autoregulation; contextual rather than BHOC efficacy evidence.

references.label: McGovern and colleagues: Hypoxia and neutrophil antimicrobial function
references.detail: Human-cell study, 2011. Oxygen-dependent bacterial killing; provides biological context, not BHOC immune-efficacy evidence.

references.label: Jonsson and colleagues: Tissue oxygenation and wound healing
references.detail: Human surgical-patient study, 1991. Tissue oxygen tension, perfusion and collagen deposition; not a BHOC or veterinary rehabilitation trial.

references.label: Hughes and colleagues: Hematologic effects of HBOC-201
references.detail: Randomized single-dose study in 24 healthy adults after phlebotomy, 1995. Serum iron, ferritin and erythropoietin findings provide a research rationale; they do not establish BHOC-mediated erythropoiesis or veterinary benefit.
